title: Adapter
summary: Wrap a foreign interface so existing code can call it as if it were local.

parts.rule: Adapter translates one interface into another the client already expects. It sits at the boundary between your code and a library, legacy API, or vendor SDK. The client stays unchanged; only the adapter knows the foreign shapes and field mappings.
parts.why: Rewriting your core to match every vendor API couples you forever. Adapters localize that pain at the edge. Interviewers want the boundary named, not a fantasy rewrite of the vendor.
parts.example: Your app expects EnergySensor.readCelsius. A vendor SDK offers VendorMeter.fetchTempF. VendorMeterAdapter implements EnergySensor, calls fetchTempF, converts Fahrenheit to Celsius, and returns. Clients keep using EnergySensor. Switch vendors by writing a new adapter; clients do not change. Another case: adapt a legacy payment library that wants XML into your PayPort.charge(Money) interface by mapping fields inside LegacyPayAdapter and parsing the XML response back to a result object. body:
Rule. Adapter translates one interface into another the client already expects. It sits at the boundary between your code and a library, legacy API, or vendor SDK. The client stays unchanged; only the adapter knows the foreign shapes and field mappings.

Why it matters. Rewriting your core to match every vendor API couples you forever. Adapters localize that pain at the edge. Interviewers want the boundary named, not a fantasy rewrite of the vendor.

Worked example. Your app expects EnergySensor.readCelsius. A vendor SDK offers VendorMeter.fetchTempF. VendorMeterAdapter implements EnergySensor, calls fetchTempF, converts Fahrenheit to Celsius, and returns. Clients keep using EnergySensor. Switch vendors by writing a new adapter; clients do not change. Another case: adapt a legacy payment library that wants XML into your PayPort.charge(Money) interface by mapping fields inside LegacyPayAdapter and parsing the XML response back to a result object. When to use. Use adapters at system edges: third-party SDKs, legacy services, and format mismatches. Use them to preserve a clean domain interface under your control.

When to refuse. Refuse an adapter when you own both sides and can change the callee. Refuse stacking adapters instead of fixing the boundary. Refuse putting business rules inside adapters beyond mapping. Refuse calling every wrapper an adapter when it is just a helper function.
